column11: derived and found to be nil: AbbVie generated $17,816mm of free cash flow on $61,160mm of revenue in FY2025, a 29.13% margin, against the 28.95% its cost of sales, SG&A and R&D leave. The two reconcile to within a fifth of a point, which is why this is zero rather than absent: the check was run and it found nothing to charge. Restated before interest: ABBV paid $3,002mm of interest inside operating cash flow over 2025, 4.91% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so adding it back only widens a gap the filed lines already leave, and the charge stays nil. Restated at replacement capex: ABBV spent $1,214mm on plant over 2025 against $762mm of plant depreciation, 0.74% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge stays nil. Checked without one-off cash: deal payments are booked under investing, so free cash flow never carried them, and no settlement or transition tax is stated for the window, so the charge stands. Restated to the amortisation floor: the filed cost lines leave a 32.46% pre-tax margin where the cash over 2025 supports 38.40%, so the charge rebuilds at -5.94%. It was held at nil, but ABBV books $7,377mm of non-cash amortisation of acquired intangibles inside cost of sales in FY2025 (0001551152-26-000008), 12.06% of revenue, so the charge takes the rebuilt figure: -5.94%. Restated without working capital build: over 2025 ABBV's cash flow statement shows receivables up $1,490mm, inventories up $234mm, payables and accrued liabilities up $951mm, a working capital build of $773mm, 1.26% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge falls from -5.94% to -7.35%.
column12: AbbVie books its amortisation of acquired intangibles inside cost of sales, $7,377mm of it, which is why its 29.8% cost of sales is so far above Pfizer's 25.7% and why the same test that charged Pfizer 22% charges AbbVie nothing. The older windows would imply a credit, not a cost: 33.6% over three years and 36.3% over five, both above the model, because they carry peak Humira. A backward window cannot be used to charge a company whose margin is falling

column11: one published share against the study's own criteria. NCT06345339 requires participants to 'Be on continuous thyroid replacement therapy of synthetic T4 for primary hypothyroidism for at least 12 months immediately prior to the Screening Visit' at a stable FDA-approved daily dose of at least 25 mcg. In the Optum claims arm of the study cited above, 'more than 78% of patients received thyroxine (T4) monotherapy' (Wyne KL et al., J Endocr Soc 2022;7(1):bvac172). 0.78 is the floor of that statement, about 24,364,437 patients
column12: the floor is taken rather than a point estimate because the paper states the share as 'more than 78%'. Three of the study's filters are NOT cut, for want of published shares: primary rather than secondary hypothyroidism, a documented in-range thyroid-stimulating hormone at screening and at an earlier visit, and the exclusion of conditions or surgery affecting absorption. The row is a ceiling on all three and errs high. Pushing the other way, the same paper reports untreated hypothyroidism rising from 11.8% to 14.4% of diagnosed patients over 2012 to 2019, so the untreated share is larger than the T4-monotherapy complement and some of that is upside on diagnosis rather than pool

column12: the judgement inside the anchor is that an approved Armour Thyroid takes the whole desiccated-thyroid class rather than its own 0.7004% of it, because the rival extracts are unapproved and an approved competitor changes their position. Which way it errs: low, if the class keeps growing as the new-start data say it is, since desiccated thyroid extract was 10.2% of new thyroid-hormone prescriptions in 2020, up from 5.4% in 2010, across an average 47,711 adults a year starting a new prescription in a national patient claims dataset (Ettleson MD, Ibarra S, Wan W, Peterson S, Laiteerapong N, Bianco AC, 'Demographic, Healthcare Access, and Dietary Factors Associated With Thyroid Hormone Treatments for Hypothyroidism', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(12):e1614-e1623, doi 10.1210/clinem/dgad331, PMID 37327351). High, if approval does not move prescribing and Armour keeps only what it already has. A beneficiary who filled both a levothyroxine and an extract in 2024 is counted on both sides, which inflates the denominator more than the numerator and so errs low again

column11: measured on the product's own patients, the days covered route amgn_lumakras.csv uses: CMS Medicare Part D Prescribers by Geography and Drug, data year 2024 (data.cms.gov dataset 9b4c142c-69cc-4a96-a09a-7cf2ba7f5816, national row, Brnd_Name Armour Thyroid, Gnrc_Name 'Thyroid,pork', read 2026-11-10): 660,612.6 standardised 30-day fills over 72,538 beneficiaries, so 660,612.6 x 30 / (72,538 x 365) = 0.748531 of a year supplied and 1 - 0.748531 = 0.251469. That is 273.2 days of supply a beneficiary. Medicare Part D only, 2024. A 30-day fill is a days-supply unit, so tablet strength does not enter it, which matters here because Armour Thyroid is sold in eight strengths and the label doses it in milligrams a day, 'Maintenance dosages 60 to 120 mg/day' (openFDA drug/label, set id 227e445c-b03d-44a3-b911-f00d3b2e118f). The series is 0.2664 (2020), 0.2550, 0.2548, 0.2299, 0.2515 (2024). Published cross-check: Hepp Z, Wyne K, Manthena SR, Wang S, Gossain V, 'Adherence to thyroid hormone replacement therapy: a retrospective, claims database analysis', Curr Med Res Opin 2018;34(9):1673-1678 (doi 10.1080/03007995.2018.1486293, PMID 29874941), 580,331 commercially insured US adults initiating levothyroxine: 'At 6 months, 40.3% of patients were found to be non-adherent, while 51.9% were non-adherent at 12 months', non-adherent being a proportion of days covered under 80%
column12: the price row is the Spending by Drug file and this is the Prescribers file, which count beneficiaries differently (72,568 and 72,538 in 2024, a gap of 30). The two counts are never added into one figure: the ratio here is struck inside the Prescribers file alone, as amgn_lumakras.csv strikes it. CMS calls Tot_30day_Fills a standardised fill count, so this is the share of a beneficiary's year the drug was supplied for rather than a measured proportion of days covered, and a patient who holds a stockpile or splits a tablet reads as stopping. For a lifelong daily replacement 25% a year is high as a reading of true stopping; what the row honestly says is how much of the year Medicare paid for, and it is the rate paired with a per-beneficiary price, which is what makes the stock times the price reproduce the file's own spend. The dosage units give a different reading on the same year, 21,562,205.25 units over 72,568 beneficiaries is 297.1 tablets against 365 for one a day, 0.186 stopping; the days supply route is taken because it needs no tablets-a-day assumption and the two files disagree by 8.8% on how much of a year a beneficiary gets
